newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks to publish names on Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks to publish names on Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Swiss banks will publish the names of holders of bank accounts opened before 1945 which have been identified as dormant, the Swiss Bankers' Association (SBA) said on Thursday.

The SBA said it hoped the move could be made soon, but also emphasised that the decision would affect only those accounts from that time period. It said the move would entail global publication of account holders' names. It did not say how many accounts were likely to be published.
Swiss banks conducted one search for dormant accounts in 1962, which turned up about 10 million Swiss francs ($6.8 million).
In 1995, under pressure from Jewish groups, they searched again and found another 40 million francs.
The amount was seen linked to around 800 dormant accounts.
The latest decision was communicated already to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato. He responded on Wednesday by saying: "It's about time."

The decision is being made amid allegations that Swiss banks have concealed information which could help Holocaust victims and their families recover missing assets left in Switzerland after World War II.

Copies of the letter, translated into English, were faxed to news agencies. The letter was accompanied by a copy of a letter signed by Thomas Borer, the Swiss diplomat acting as liaison in matters pertaining to the Holocaust, addressed to D'Amato. Borer's letter refered to an earlier query from D'Amato dated in March, pertaining to the dormant accounts.
The Bankers' Association letter, addressed to the Swiss Federal Banking Commission, and signed by Bankers' Association chairman Georg Krayer and board member Jean-Paul Chapuis, said:

"I am willing to express the SBA's unequivocal support for the concept of public disclosure of the names of account holders in the very special and limited circumstances presented by Holocaust-related dormant assets."
The efforts would help investigations into the period being led by a committee headed by former Federal Reserve Board chairman Paul Volcker.

"It is our hope that working with the Federal Banking Commission, the Swiss Government and other interested parties including the Volcker Commission, a mechanism will be implemented soon that will permit such disclosure consistent with Swiss law and sound banking practices," the letter said.
It said the three largest Swiss banks, Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corp and Union Bank of Switzerland supported the decision.
The institutions had agreed to sharing the cost required to publicise the list of account holders' names, it added.
